goal.objective:
`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `normalize` or `resolve`, reads UTF-8 text from standard input, and writes one result line per input line to standard output. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves; every remaining line is a record, including an empty one. Exit 0 when every record succeeds.

In `normalize` mode each record is one URI reference and its output line is the normalized form. In `resolve` mode each record is a base URI, one space, and a reference; the output line is the reference resolved against the base and then normalized. The first space separates the two, so a reference may contain spaces and a base may not.

Parse a URI reference into scheme, authority, path, query and fragment by RFC 3986's generic syntax: an optional scheme running to the first `:`, which may not be preceded by any `/`, `?` or `#`; an optional authority introduced by `//` and running to the next `/`, `?` or `#`; the path up to the next `?` or `#`; an optional query from `?` to the next `#`; an optional fragment from `#` to the end. An absent component and an empty one are different, so `http://a/b?` has an empty query, `http://a/b` has none, and both print back the way they came. Inside an authority the userinfo is everything before the last `@`, the port is everything after the first `:` that follows the last `]`, and the host is what lies between.

Normalization applies in this order. Lowercase the scheme, using ASCII rules only. Normalize percent-encodings in every component: uppercase the two hexadecimal digits of each `%XX`, then replace the triplet with the character it encodes when that character is unreserved, meaning one of `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `-`, `.`, `_` and `~`. Lowercase the host, using ASCII rules only and leaving the userinfo alone. Drop the port when it is written empty or written with exactly the digits of the scheme's default, which is 80 for `http` and `ws`, 443 for `https` and `wss`, and 21 for `ftp`; no other scheme has one, and a port padded with a leading zero is not written with those digits and stays. Remove dot segments from the path by RFC 3986 section 5.2.4, so a `.` segment disappears, a `..` segment removes the segment before it, and a `..` that would climb above the root is discarded. Finally, when an authority is present and the path is empty, make the path `/`. Dot removal never touches the query or the fragment.

Resolve by RFC 3986 section 5.2.2 in its strict form, in which a reference that repeats the base's scheme is still an absolute URI. A reference that writes a scheme is itself the target, with the dot segments removed from its path. A reference that writes an authority takes the base's scheme and keeps everything else of its own. A reference with neither and an empty path takes the base's authority and path, takes the base's query only when it writes no query of its own, and takes its own fragment, which may be absent. Otherwise, when the reference's path does not start with `/`, merge it onto the base's: keep everything of the base path up to and including its last `/`, or use the reference path alone when the base path holds no `/`, except that a base that has an authority and an empty path contributes a single leading `/`. Remove the dot segments from the resulting path, take the base's authority and the reference's query and fragment, and normalize the whole.

A failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; stop at the first one. The messages are `error: usage: cli.js normalize|resolve` when the arguments are not exactly one of the two mode words; `error: line N: expected a base and a reference` when a `resolve` record holds no space; `error: line N: the base has no scheme` when the base of a `resolve` record writes no scheme; and `error: line N: the path has a truncated percent-encoding` when a `%` is not followed by two hexadecimal digits, with `path` replaced by `userinfo`, `host`, `query` or `fragment` for whichever component carries it, those five being checked in that order. N counts records from 1. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root. This task is also judged on inputs you do not see: a validator runs your program on its own held-back cases and compares the exit code and output byte for byte. The visible tests cover the main paths only. Implement the written specification, including every corner it states, rather than the behaviour the visible tests happen to pin down.

<system-reminder>
A skill is a reusable set of task-specific instructions. The following skills are available in this session:

<available_skills>
- `dsh-archive-agent-notes`: Use when adding, auditing, pruning, archiving, restoring, or reviewing Agent Notes in deepseek-harness; checks every new note for superseded active records, classifies implemented notes by future decision value, deletes rejected notes that no longer prevent a tempting fallacy, and applies the frozen archived/{kind} triplet and manifest rules.
- `dsh-code-review`: Use when reviewing a pull request in the deepseek-harness repo — orients the reviewer to this codebase's standards (AGENTS.md conventions, defensive patterns, ADRs, quality gates) and the review-specific checks that code alone can't show
- `dsh-doc-site-sync`: Use when publishing, updating, moving, or removing DeepSeek Harness documentation website pages; editing website/docs.ts mappings or navigation; diagnosing a page missing from the VitePress site; fixing projected documentation links; or running the docs:dev, docs:check, and doc-sync workflow after website-content changes.
- `dsh-doc-standards`: Use when writing, moving, reviewing, or auditing documentation in the deepseek-harness repo — choosing hierarchy and detail, separating tutorials from references, checking tutorial progression, trimming doc slop, responding to a verify-doc-budgets failure, or requests like "improve the docs", "audit the docs", "where should this be documented", or "this doc is too long".
- `dsh-find-simplifications`: Use when working in the deepseek-harness repo to find non-obvious simplification candidates, write proposed Agent Notes or inline TODO/FIXME/XXX notes, audit or coalesce superseded Agent Notes, or fold worthwhile simplification ideas from another PR; especially for dead, duplicated, speculative, over-built, added-then-removed, or hand-rolled-where-a-dependency-exists surfaces.
- `dsh-merging-stacked-prs`: Use when landing a stack of dependent GitHub PRs (A ← B ← C, where each bases on the one below) onto master, merging a PR whose base is another open PR's branch, or whenever a request mentions "stacked PRs", "PR stack", "dependent PRs", or merging several related PRs in sequence. Requires every same-repository dependency chain to use GitHub's official stacked-PR feature before landing so GitHub owns stack-wide rules, CI, ordering, retargeting, and merge state.
- `dsh-pre-push-checks`: Use before pushing, force-pushing, marking ready for review, or claiming checks pass on a deepseek-harness branch, and immediately after gh stack sync publishes rewritten branches, to select the smallest tests and checks that cover the outgoing or just-published diff without reflexively running the full repository suite.
- `dsh-prose-standard`: Use when writing, reviewing, restoring, trimming, or auditing prose in the deepseek-harness repo, including deciding where documentation or comments are required across Markdown, JSDoc, code and test comments, prompts, descriptions, diagnostics, and CLI or UI strings.
- `dsh-trim-cot-leakage`: Use when auditing or fixing prose that reads like a leaked reasoning transcript — dead design-session citations such as (decision N), audit item codes, or §N of uncommitted drafts; change narration such as "used to", "no longer", "this cut"; stack or review vantage ("a later PR in this stack", "rejected in review"); reviewer-addressed justifications; control-flow narration; or hedged planning residue in comments, JSDoc, docs, or Agent Notes.
- `record-browser-gif`: Record browser or Web UI interaction demos as optimized GIFs using the available built-in browser, state-based frame capture, and deterministic encoding, then publish to a dedicated assets branch when the task includes attaching the GIF to a pull request. Use when asked to make, record, or generate a GIF that demonstrates a browser workflow, and for every pull request that changes product-user-visible GUI behavior, which MUST include a GIF recorded from the pull request's real server and mode...
</available_skills>

If the user names a skill, or the task clearly matches a skill's description, call the `skill` tool with the exact skill name before taking task actions. Load all applicable skills, then follow their full instructions. This catalog contains summaries only; do not infer or follow a skill's instructions until it has been loaded.
A user may also invoke a skill directly; its <skill_content> block then appears in this conversation. Follow it, and do not call the `skill` tool again for that skill.
</system-reminder>

header.system:
You are an AI agent powered by DeepSeek Harness.

You implement one program task in the workspace you are given, against its own test suite, and you stop when the tests pass.

The workspace is your working directory: every bash command and every file path resolves inside it, so read and edit its files by their relative paths and never search outside it.


Use the read tool — not shell commands like cat — to inspect text files. Results include line numbers. Use offset and limit to continue reading large files.

Use the write tool to create files or completely replace file contents. Existing files are overwritten, so read an existing file first (the default fs-observation-policy requires it) and prefer edit for targeted changes.

Use the edit tool for targeted changes to existing UTF-8 text files. It replaces literal old_string with new_string; by default old_string must appear exactly once. If old_string appears multiple times, provide a more specific old_string or set replace_all to true. Read the file first (the default fs-observation-policy requires it), unless you just created or edited it in this session.

Check the [exit code: N] marker on every bash result; investigate failures before moving on.

Track every background job id you start. You are notified in-session when a job finishes — do not busy-poll or sleep on one; keep working on independent steps and do not duplicate a running job's work. Before giving a final answer, collect every still-relevant job with job_output (set wait: true only when you are genuinely blocked on it), and job_kill jobs that stopped mattering.

tools.name: bash
tools.description: Execute a bash command (`bash -c`) and return its stdout/stderr. Each call runs in a fresh shell: no state (cwd, variables, functions) persists between calls — pass `workdir` instead of using `cd`. Non-zero exits are reported as `[exit code: N]`. Current harness environment facts are exposed through managed `$DSH_*` variables; inspect them when needed. Commands may run under a file sandbox; a blocked file operation is reported as `[sandbox: file access denied under <mode> mode]` — a policy denial, not a bug in the command; do not retry another way. Long output is truncated to its tail; the full output is saved to a file whose path is reported when available. Set `run_in_background: true` for long-running commands: the call returns a job id immediately; read its output with `job_output` and stop it with `job_kill`. Attempting a command the sandbox may deny is safe and expected: run it and read the marker rather than assuming the denial. When a command is denied and a wider mode would let it succeed, escalate immediately in the same turn — the one sanctioned exception to a denial: retry the exact same command once with `sandbox_permissions` (the narrowest wider mode that suffices) plus a one-sentence `justification`. Do not detour through chat to ask permission first — the approval prompt raised by that retry is how the user consents. If the session states approval prompts are disabled, there is no exception: a denial is final — do not set `sandbox_permissions`. Never escalate speculatively: ground the request in a real denial — normally the one this command just hit; escalating up front is fine only when this session already denied the same access. A rejected escalation is final for that command — stop and explain, never work around it — but it does not forbid attempting or escalating other commands later.

description.description: Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice, 5-10 words (shown in the UI). Examples: "ls" → "List files in current directory"; "git status" → "Show working tree status"; "npm install" → "Install package dependencies".

timeoutMs.description: Timeout in milliseconds. The executor applies its configured default and cap, and kills the command on expiry.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path is resolved against it.

run_in_background.description: Run in the background and return a job id immediately (collect with job_output, stop with job_kill). No timeout applies.

sandbox_permissions.description: The wider sandbox mode this command needs. Only valid as a one-shot retry of a command the sandbox just denied; requires justification and user approval.

justification.description: Required with sandbox_permissions: one sentence for the user explaining why this exact command needs the wider access.

tools.name: edit
tools.description: Edit an existing UTF-8 text file by replacing literal text.

file_path.description: Path to edit, resolved by the filesystem backend.

old_string.description: Literal text to replace. Must match exactly.

new_string.description: Literal replacement text. Use an empty string to delete the match.

replace_all.description: Replace all matches. Defaults to false; when false, old_string must appear exactly once.

tools.name: job_kill
tools.description: Request cancellation of a running background job by job id. Returns immediately; the job settles as killed once its work actually stops.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

reason.description: Optional short reason, recorded in the log and forwarded to the job.

tools.name: job_list
tools.description: List your background jobs (running and finished) with their ids, kinds, and statuses.

tools.name: job_output
tools.description: Read a background job. Stream jobs return only output since the previous read; final-output jobs return their result after settlement. Every response ends with `[status: ...]`. Reads are non-blocking unless `wait: true`, which waits up to the configured cap.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

wait.description: Block until the job reaches a terminal status or the timeout expires. A timed-out wait returns [status: running] and leaves the job alive.

timeout_ms.description: Max wait in milliseconds (only meaningful with wait: true). Defaults to the configured wait timeout; capped by the configured maximum.

tools.name: read
tools.description: Read a UTF-8 text file and return line-numbered content.

file_path.description: Path to read, resolved by the filesystem backend.

offset.description: 1-based first line to return. Defaults to 1.

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to return. Defaults to 2000.

tools.name: skill
tools.description: Load the full instructions for an available skill. Call this with the exact skill name from the session skill catalog before acting on a task that names or clearly matches that skill.

name.description: The exact skill name from the available skills list.

tools.description: Create or fully replace a UTF-8 text file.

file_path.description: Path to write, resolved by the filesystem backend.

content.description: Full UTF-8 text content to write.

## Summary

Implemented the `normalize`/`resolve` CLI across two files under `src/`:

- **`src/uri.js`** — pure logic: `parseUriReference` (scheme/authority/path/query/fragment splitting, plus authority's userinfo/host/port splitting, all per the stated RFC 3986 generic-syntax rules with absent-vs-empty component tracking), `serialize`, `removeDotSegments` (RFC 3986 §5.2.4), `normalize` (lowercases scheme, decodes unreserved percent-triplets while uppercasing hex digits elsewhere, lowercases host, drops empty/default ports, removes dot segments, roots an empty path when an authority is present — in the specified order, validating percent-encodings first in path→userinfo→host→query→fragment order), and `resolveReference` (strict RFC 3986 §5.2.2, including the merge-path special case for an authority with an empty base path).
- **`src/cli.js`** — argument/usage validation, stdin reading, record splitting (dropping only the trailing empty element a final newline produces), per-line dispatch to normalize or resolve, and the specified error messages/exit codes, stopping output entirely on the first failing line.

Verified against the visible test suite (`node --test test/*.test.js`, 16/16 passing) and manually against spec corners not covered by the visible tests: absent-vs-empty query/authority round-tripping, padded (non-default) ports being kept, percent-encoding truncation error ordering across components, usage errors for wrong argument counts, dot-segment climb-above-root discarding, and empty-path-with-authority rooting.

No dependencies were added and `test/`/`package.json` were left untouched.

goal.objective:
`src/cli.js` is the program; how the work is split across other files under `src/` is up to you. It takes exactly one argument, `normalize` or `resolve`, reads UTF-8 text from standard input, and writes one result line per input line to standard output. Split the input on newlines and drop the empty tail a trailing newline leaves; every remaining line is a record, including an empty one. Exit 0 when every record succeeds.

In `normalize` mode each record is one URI reference and its output line is the normalized form. In `resolve` mode each record is a base URI, one space, and a reference; the output line is the reference resolved against the base and then normalized. The first space separates the two, so a reference may contain spaces and a base may not.

Parse a URI reference into scheme, authority, path, query and fragment by RFC 3986's generic syntax: an optional scheme running to the first `:`, which may not be preceded by any `/`, `?` or `#`; an optional authority introduced by `//` and running to the next `/`, `?` or `#`; the path up to the next `?` or `#`; an optional query from `?` to the next `#`; an optional fragment from `#` to the end. An absent component and an empty one are different, so `http://a/b?` has an empty query, `http://a/b` has none, and both print back the way they came. Inside an authority the userinfo is everything before the last `@`, the port is everything after the first `:` that follows the last `]`, and the host is what lies between.

Normalization applies in this order. Lowercase the scheme, using ASCII rules only. Normalize percent-encodings in every component: uppercase the two hexadecimal digits of each `%XX`, then replace the triplet with the character it encodes when that character is unreserved, meaning one of `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `-`, `.`, `_` and `~`. Lowercase the host, using ASCII rules only and leaving the userinfo alone. Drop the port when it is written empty or written with exactly the digits of the scheme's default, which is 80 for `http` and `ws`, 443 for `https` and `wss`, and 21 for `ftp`; no other scheme has one, and a port padded with a leading zero is not written with those digits and stays. Remove dot segments from the path by RFC 3986 section 5.2.4, so a `.` segment disappears, a `..` segment removes the segment before it, and a `..` that would climb above the root is discarded. Finally, when an authority is present and the path is empty, make the path `/`. Dot removal never touches the query or the fragment.

Resolve by RFC 3986 section 5.2.2 in its strict form, in which a reference that repeats the base's scheme is still an absolute URI. A reference that writes a scheme is itself the target, with the dot segments removed from its path. A reference that writes an authority takes the base's scheme and keeps everything else of its own. A reference with neither and an empty path takes the base's authority and path, takes the base's query only when it writes no query of its own, and takes its own fragment, which may be absent. Otherwise, when the reference's path does not start with `/`, merge it onto the base's: keep everything of the base path up to and including its last `/`, or use the reference path alone when the base path holds no `/`, except that a base that has an authority and an empty path contributes a single leading `/`. Remove the dot segments from the resulting path, take the base's authority and the reference's query and fragment, and normalize the whole.

A failure writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; stop at the first one. The messages are `error: usage: cli.js normalize|resolve` when the arguments are not exactly one of the two mode words; `error: line N: expected a base and a reference` when a `resolve` record holds no space; `error: line N: the base has no scheme` when the base of a `resolve` record writes no scheme; and `error: line N: the path has a truncated percent-encoding` when a `%` is not followed by two hexadecimal digits, with `path` replaced by `userinfo`, `host`, `query` or `fragment` for whichever component carries it, those five being checked in that order. N counts records from 1. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root. This task is also judged on inputs you do not see: a validator runs your program on its own held-back cases and compares the exit code and output byte for byte. The visible tests cover the main paths only. Implement the written specification, including every corner it states, rather than the behaviour the visible tests happen to pin down.
